title: Political identity is emerging as a health determinant through trust, care engagement, and mortality divergence
source_unit: Nature Human Behaviour article by Elizabeth Elder and Neil A. O’Brian (2026); Add Health longitudinal medical, biomarker, and death-record analysis plus an original medical-engagement survey (N=21,751)
geography: United States; nationally representative longitudinal cohort and a separately weighted online opinion sample

observations.period: Before the 2010s through 2020–2022; political divergence in health and mortality

denominator.unit: reported comparison between self-identified liberal and conservative Americans in the Add Health cohort

health_and_mortality_gap.value: no significant gap before the 2010s; worse health and higher mortality among conservatives during the 2010s and by the 2020s

observations.method: Individual-level medical data and death records from Add Health, including repeated political-orientation measures and National Death Index follow-up through 2022.
observations.uncertainty: The study is observational and uses self-reported liberal–conservative placement rather than a directly usable party-identification or vote-choice measure; mortality is rare in this relatively young cohort.
observations.subgroup: Add Health participants born predominantly between 1977 and 1982; comparisons use self-identified political orientation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cohort composition, geography, occupation, education, institutional context, health selection, and unmeasured factors may contribute to the divergence; the result does not show that ideology alone causes mortality.

medical_and_biomarker_scope.value: body mass index, lipids/cholesterol, HbA1c, blood pressure, C-reactive protein, and vital status
medical_and_biomarker_scope.unit: five biomarkers plus National Death Index linkage

observations.method: In-home clinical measurements in Add Health waves 4 and 5, with death-record linkage through 2022.
observations.uncertainty: The measures improve on purely ecological comparisons but do not establish the causal pathway from political identity to biological change or death.
observations.subgroup: Mostly adults aged roughly 40–45 by 2021–2022 in the wave 5 cohort.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed biomarkers and mortality can reflect accumulated social, economic, geographic, behavioral, and institutional exposures that correlate with political orientation.

explanatory_boundary.value: demographic realignment explains some of the gap, but demographic change, public policy, and COVID-19 do not fully account for the widening mortality difference

observations.method: Longitudinal comparisons and additional analyses described in the peer-reviewed article.
observations.uncertainty: This is an interpretation of the evidence, not a complete causal decomposition; remaining explanations may include selection, local context, behavior, and institutional trust.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults in the Add Health comparison universe.
observations.counterinterpretation: Residual confounding and period/cohort effects may account for some of the remaining association; the article does not identify a single sufficient mechanism.

observations.period: Contemporary survey; political differences in medical engagement

denominator.unit: respondents in the original online survey, weighted to approximate national demographics

medical_trust_and_engagement.value: right-leaning individuals show lower willingness to seek care, follow clinical advice, and believe medication is effective, including for issues unrelated to COVID-19

observations.method: Original online survey measuring willingness to engage with the medical system, analyzed against ideology, partisanship, and vote choice.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is cross-sectional and was fielded after the Add Health outcome period, so it cannot directly test trust as the cause of the historical mortality divergence; the authors describe the mechanism as evidence-consistent, not proven causal.
observations.subgroup: Contemporary U.S. survey respondents, weighted to approximate national demographics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Differences may reflect broader institutional distrust, healthcare access, experiences of treatment, media environments, or political sorting rather than ideology operating independently.

related_sources.claim: Publisher DOI for the peer-reviewed Nature Human Behaviour article.
PubMed bibliographic record for the article.

boundary: This record identifies a U.S. trend in which political identity may be becoming a social determinant of health through trust and medical-care engagement. It does not establish that ideology causes mortality, that one party’s beliefs determine health, or that trust is the sole explanation for the observed divergence.
